title: Lecture #2: Write Your First JAVA Program

questions.question: According to the lecture, what does the JRE (Java Runtime Environment) consist of?
options: The JVM plus the class libraries that programs use for things like console output and file reading
The compiler, debugger and Javadoc tool
Only the JIT compiler, without an interpreter
The JDK plus an IDE such as VS Code or IntelliJ
questions.explanation: The notes give JRE = JVM + class libraries, the ready-made code your program calls for console output, file reading, etc. The compiler, debugger and Javadoc belong to the JDK, which is the outermost circle (JDK = JRE + development tools).

questions.question: The lecture contrasts C/C++, Python and Java. Which classification matches the notes?
options: C/C++ is interpreted, Python is compiled, Java is compiled only
All three are purely compiled languages
C/C++ is compiled, Python is interpreted, Java is purely interpreted
C/C++ is compiled, Python is interpreted, Java is both compiled and interpreted
questions.explanation: A compiler converts the whole code at once and an interpreter converts line by line; C/C++ use a compiler and Python an interpreter. Java uses both: javac compiles source to bytecode, and the JVM then runs that bytecode with an interpreter (helped by the JIT), so calling it 'purely interpreted' ignores the compile step.

questions.question: You are setting up a new laptop to write, compile and debug your own Java programs. Which one should you install?
options: Only a JVM, because it is the part that runs bytecode
The JDK, because it contains the JRE plus the compiler, debugger and other development tools
Only the JRE, because it already includes the javac compiler
Only an IDE such as IntelliJ, because IDEs replace the need for Java
questions.explanation: Developing means compiling, and the compiler (plus debugger, Javadoc) is in the JDK, which also contains the JRE and JVM to run the result. The JRE can only run already-compiled programs; it does not contain javac.

questions.question: You run the two commands below in the folder containing `Demo.java`. What does the second command actually load and execute?
options: Demo.java, which the java command re-reads line by line as source text
A Demo.exe file that javac created for your operating system
Demo.class, whose bytecode the JVM in the JRE converts to machine code for the CPU
Nothing; the second command only checks Demo.java for syntax errors
questions.explanation: The notes show Demo.java -> javac -> Demo.class (bytecode) -> `java Demo` -> JRE/JVM -> machine code -> CPU -> output. Note that `java Demo` takes the class name and uses the compiled Demo.class; javac never produces a native .exe.

questions.question: The lecture lists the main jobs of the JVM. Which of the following is NOT one of the JVM's jobs?
options: Compiling Demo.java source code into Demo.class bytecode
Converting bytecode into machine code using an interpreter and a JIT compiler
Providing security by running code inside a sandbox model
Garbage collection, i.e. freeing memory that is no longer used
questions.explanation: The notes list the JVM's jobs as (1) bytecode -> machine code via interpreter + JIT, (2) security via the sandbox model, (3) garbage collection. Turning .java source into bytecode is done by javac, a JDK tool that runs before the JVM is ever involved.

questions.question: A beginner compiles successfully and then types the second command below (Java 17). What happens?
options: The program runs normally, because the .class extension is optional
javac runs again and recompiles Demo.java before running it
The JVM runs Demo.java directly in source-file mode
It fails with "Could not find or load main class Demo.class", because `java` expects the class name, not the file name
questions.explanation: The `java` launcher takes a class name (`java Demo`), so `Demo.class` is treated as a class named `class` inside a package `Demo`, which does not exist, giving ClassNotFoundException. Source-file mode only applies when you pass a `.java` file, not a `.class` file.

questions.question: Your team is building a large, transactional banking web application for enterprise use. Which Java edition from the lecture is designed for this kind of system?
options: JME (Java Micro Edition), because banking apps run on phones
JEE (Java Enterprise Edition), now called Jakarta EE
JSE (Java Standard Edition) only, because enterprise features do not exist
JRE, because enterprise apps only need a runtime
questions.explanation: The notes map JSE = core Java, JEE = enterprise/transactional systems (renamed Jakarta EE), and JME = lightweight devices (linked to Android-era mobile). JEE builds on JSE, so 'JSE only' misses the enterprise APIs, and the JRE is a runtime, not an edition.

questions.question: A production server has only a Java runtime (JRE) installed. A teammate logs in and runs `javac App.java`, but the shell says `javac: command not found`. What is the right fix?
options: Reinstall the JRE, because its JVM must be corrupted
Run `java App.java` with the JRE's built-in compiler instead of javac
Compile on a machine with a JDK and deploy the compiled .class files, or install a JDK on the server
Rename App.java to App.class so the JRE can run it
questions.explanation: javac is a development tool that ships in the JDK (JDK = JRE + compiler, debugger, ...); a JRE can only run bytecode. Renaming a file does not create bytecode, and nothing is wrong with the JVM; the compiler is simply not part of a runtime-only install.

questions.question: In the program below, `square` is called one million times. Based on the lecture's model of the JVM, what happens to `square` while the program runs?
options: javac compiles square directly to machine code, so the JVM never interprets it
It is first interpreted, then the JIT compiler detects it as frequently executed code and compiles it to machine code that is reused for later calls
The JIT compiler translates the whole program to machine code before main starts, like a C++ compiler
The interpreter re-translates square on every one of the million calls; the JIT is only used for code that runs once
questions.explanation: The notes show bytecode going to the interpreter, while frequent code is sent to the JIT, whose machine code is then reused, which is why the JVM = interpreter + JIT. The JIT works at runtime on hot code, not ahead of time on the whole program, and javac only ever produces bytecode.

questions.question: Why does the JVM combine an interpreter with a JIT compiler instead of JIT-compiling every method as soon as the program starts?
options: Compiling costs time and memory, so it pays off only for frequently executed code; code that runs rarely is cheaper to just interpret
The JIT compiler can only compile methods named main
Interpreted code is always faster than compiled machine code
Compiling everything up front would make the bytecode platform dependent
questions.explanation: The notes tie this design to early constraints (slow hardware, limited RAM, slow disk): translating everything up front was expensive, so the JVM interprets by default and JIT-compiles only the frequent code. Interpreted code is slower, not faster, which is why hot code gets compiled at all.
